query: For high-value components operating in aggressive environments, what intervention could improve surface physical and mechanical characteristics? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence that would support it, and an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled thermal annealing of high-entropy alloy (HEA) surfaces (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo films) induces the formation of a dense, protective composite oxide layer that improves surface hardness, wear resistance, and oxidation resistance in aggressive high-temperature environments relative to untreated surfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited HEA films with a relatively porous or less-stable microstructure that lacks a fully developed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA film to controlled thermal annealing (thermal shock) at approximately 800 °C for 1 hour in air.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, oxidative, and mechanically abrasive environments typical of aggressive service conditions encountered by high-value components.
generation.structural_mediator: The thermal annealing promotes inter-diffusion and reaction between alloy elements to form a dense composite oxide layer (such as ZrTiO4) that passivates the surface and refines the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Annealing accelerates diffusion processes that lead to the formation of a compact, adherent oxide layer, reducing surface defects. This layer limits further oxidation and minimizes wear by increasing surface hardness and lowering the coefficient of friction under aggressive conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, annealed HEA films will exhibit higher hardness, lower friction (COF), reduced wear rates, and enhanced oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: As-deposited HEA films or bare alloys, which show higher wear rates, lower hardness, and less robust passive behavior when exposed to high-temperature oxidative environments.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for HEA systems with elemental compositions capable of forming stable protective oxides. Its effectiveness may diminish if the annealing temperature deviates substantially from 800 °C, if the atmosphere is non-oxidative, or for alloy compositions that cannot form a compact oxide layer.
generation.uncertainty: While prior experiments indicate improved tribocorrosion performance with annealing at 800 °C, uncertainties remain regarding the precise magnitude of improvement across different HEA systems and the optimum processing parameters for each composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA film samples (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo films). Subject one set to thermal annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour in air and leave the other set untreated. Expose both sets to a simulated aggressive environment involving high-temperature oxidation and mechanical wear using a standardized tribocorrosion test rig.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) during sliding tests
Wear rate (calculated from wear volume, load, and sliding distance)
Characterization of surface oxide layer composition and density (using XPS/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., higher hardness, lower COF, reduced wear rate, and a denser, more protective oxide layer) compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

cited_evidence.text: From Figure 10, the OCP curves of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the film annealed at 400 °C have similar changes with ΔOCP values of 0.453 and 0.461, respectively. During the rapid sliding, the two curves remain stable due to the dynamic balance between activation and passivation within the wear track [,]. Additionally, the two COFs are 0.13 and 0.09, respectively (Table 5). As shown in Figure 11a,b, many adhesions and furrows are found on the abrasion track of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the film annealed for 400 °C. The dense microstructure of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film after annealing at 600 °C and the increased H and E improve the resistance to external damage, resulting in a reduction in ΔOCP, COF and wear rate. The ΔOCP, COF and wear rate of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C are minimized to 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1, respectively, and no obvious wear characteristics appear in the abrasion track, which means that the film is not destroyed.
